Hi Sam / Priya —

Thanks again for the discovery call today — really helpful to understand the Zenly Health workload. Two quick follow-ups so we can align pricing estimates to your budget:

1) You mentioned ~200M characters / month across clinical summaries and search prompts. Can you confirm whether that number is: (a) raw characters from user text only, or (b) includes generated summaries?
2) You also asked whether we bill per request vs per token, and how prompt caching affects billed usage. I want to be explicit so your finance/comms team is comfortable.

High-level answers in short: Redwood bills on tokens (input + output). Characters are a helpful proxy (rough rule: ~4 characters = 1 token for English), and requests are just API calls — they matter for concurrency but not unit pricing. Caching can reduce billed tokens for repeated identical prompts/contexts, but it depends on how much of your traffic is repeatable.

I looped in Nikhil (SE) to give a concrete example of token/character conversion and an estimated $/1M token target based on the usage profile you described. If you can confirm whether the 200M chars is pre- or post-generation and share a small sample of typical prompts (or the sample file you mentioned), we can give a tighter cost estimate.

Hi Sam — thanks for the details. Short answers up-front: yes, Redwood billing = billed tokens = input tokens + output tokens. Requests (API calls) do not carry a per-request token surcharge, but they impact concurrency and thus performance/throughput planning.

Conversion and worked example:
- Empirical rule of thumb: English text ~4 characters per token (this varies by language and punctuation).
- Your stated 240M characters -> ~60M tokens (240M / 4).
- Billing is for tokens processed by the model. Example: if a single call uses a 200-token prompt (input) and the model generates 300 tokens (output), that call bills 500 tokens.

Prompt caching behavior (how it affects billed tokens):
- Redwood supports prefix/KV caching for repeated prefixes and identical context. Cache hits can avoid re-computation on the runtime (reducing latency and cost), but our billing still counts billed tokens unless the request can be served entirely from a persistent cache layer configured to not charge for repeated responses. 
- Practically: caching provides most benefit when (a) the entire prompt+context is identical across requests, and (b) the cached artifact is a generated response stored at the application layer (e.g., CDN or application cache).
- For your templated prompts (30% identical): if you store and re-serve the generated output at the app layer, those re-serves are free. If you're re-sending the identical prompt to the API on every user interaction, the model will execute and you will be billed for tokens (though runtime-side KV caches may reduce GPU work and latency, they don't always avoid billing unless you use Redwood's higher-level response cache feature).

Unit economics (illustrative):
- If you target $/1M tokens, here are three example bands we can use for cost planning (hosted list pricing guidance):
  * Conservative pilot tier: $60 / 1M tokens -> 60M tokens = $3,600/mo
  * Mid-tier negotiated: $30 / 1M tokens -> 60M tokens = $1,800/mo
  * Aggressive committed: $12 / 1M tokens -> 60M tokens = $720/mo

Using your ~60M token estimate:
- At $30/1M -> ~ $1,800/month (fits the $3k-$6k/mo pilot when you add overhead/throughput buffers and multiple models).
- At $12/1M -> ~ $720/month (this is a committed-dedicated pricing band and requires usage/term commitment).

Recommendations:
1) For an initial pilot, model assume 60M billed tokens / month and plan to optimize via application caching to reduce repeat generation.
2) We'll prepare a 3-tier quote: pilot (no commit), committed 6-month, and committed 12-month with step-down $/1M bands.
3) Send us two sanitized prompt examples (Marissa has the template) and we can run quick tokenization on them and return exact token counts.

I'll attach a short worksheet to show tokenized examples and sample monthly cost tables.
